partner_context.their_ambition: Beyond the resorts, the Maldives runs one of the world's most ambitious public-transport challenges: connecting ~190 inhabited islands across 20 atolls into a single integrated national ferry network so that every citizen — not just every guest — can reach a hospital, a school, a job or the capital reliably and affordably.
partner_context.their_pressure: The integrated public ferry network depends on a large fleet of diesel vessels: expensive to fuel, carbon-heavy in a nation acutely exposed to sea-level rise, and weather-limited on the longer inter-atoll legs. As the network expands island-by-island, fuel and reliability — not ambition — are the binding constraints.
partner_context.where_navier_fits: Navier offers the public network a decisive step-change: foiling-electric vessels that are faster, all-weather, near-silent and zero-emission, running on the berths and harbours that already exist. The same platform already deploying in Maldivian waters can decarbonise and speed up the resident routes — turning a fuel liability into a modern national asset.

hero.eyebrow: Authority proposal · Republic of Maldives · National Ferry Network (RTL)
hero.title: Navier × Maldives — the public ferry network, re-platformed
hero.subtitle: Decarbonising and speeding up the integrated national ferry network that connects every inhabited island.
hero.what_we_do_together: Navier works with the national network to bring foiling-electric vessels to the resident inter-atoll routes — the high-frequency island-to-island and island-to-capital legs that the integrated public ferry system runs every day. Navier supplies the software-defined fleet, captain training and the certification path; the network brings the route map, the harbour infrastructure and the public-service mandate. The result is a faster, all-weather, zero-emission public ferry layer for the residents and communities who depend on it every day.

why_now: The integrated national ferry network is expanding atoll-by-atoll on a diesel fleet, just as the Navier × JIH Global program proves — publicly, at scale — that foiling-electric vessels work in exactly these waters. The Maldives has a stated net-zero ambition and the world's most direct exposure to sea-level rise, so a zero-emission public fleet is not a nice-to-have but a strategic alignment. The proof case is already in the lagoon; the public network is the natural next layer.
multimodal_fit: The national ferry network is the backbone of resident mobility; Navier slots in as the fast, all-weather upgrade for its busiest and longest legs. Foiling vessels take the high-frequency island-to-capital and inter-atoll routes where speed and reliability matter most, while conventional craft and the existing harbour network continue to serve the shortest hops — one integrated system, decarbonised from the busiest corridors outward.

proof_points.claim: Foiling-electric is already deploying at national scale here.
proof_points.evidence: Navier × JIH Global: ~100 vessels / $100M / three-year phasing; first 5 boats in 2026.

proof_points.claim: The platform is proven in service.
proof_points.evidence: 10 vessels delivered, 4,000+ flight hours, 2025 production sold out.

proof_points.claim: The public network is large and growing.
proof_points.evidence: An integrated national ferry network linking ~190 inhabited islands across 20 atolls, expanding in phases.
proof_points.source: Government of Maldives / national ferry program

proof_points.evidence: The Maldives has a stated net-zero ambition and acute exposure to sea-level rise — a zero-emission public fleet is strategically aligned.

objections.concern: Can an electric fleet serve remote islands without charging infrastructure?
objections.response: Pioneer II needs only a berth pedestal at existing island harbours; the Quanta-LR hybrid needs no charging at all, covering the longest inter-atoll legs — so coverage is not gated on building charging at every island.

objections.concern: Is foiling reliable in monsoon conditions?
objections.response: The foil flies above the chop for a smoother, more reliable ride than a diesel ferry in the same sea state, and the all-weather, after-dark capability means fewer weather cancellations on the routes residents depend on.

objections.concern: Is this affordable for a public-service network?
objections.response: Foiling-electric is roughly 10x more efficient than a conventional planing hull, so fuel — the largest operating cost of a diesel ferry fleet — falls sharply; the same public budget reaches more islands more often.

objections.concern: Is the platform proven in Maldivian waters?
objections.response: Yes — a large foiling-electric program is already deploying at national scale in Maldivian waters, so the public network inherits a supply chain, captain training and maintenance playbook proven in exactly these conditions and sea states.

the_ask.navier_brings: The software-defined foiling fleet, captain training, the maintenance and certification path, and an operating playbook already being proven in Maldivian waters.
the_ask.partner_brings: The national ferry route map, harbour infrastructure, the public-service mandate and the phased expansion sequence across atolls.
the_ask.next_step: Identify the first resident corridors for a foiling-electric public pilot and align it with the national ferry network's expansion plan.

close.title: The same lagoon, for everyone.
close.body: The foiling platform already deploying in Maldivian waters is the same one that can give every islander a faster, all-weather, zero-emission ride to the hub. The public ferry network is how marine mobility reaches the whole nation — not just its visitors.

why_navier_now.step_change: Hydrofoiling lifts the hull clear of the water, so a Navier vessel flies instead of plowing through chop — roughly 10x more efficient than a conventional planing boat, faster (30+ kt cruise), and dramatically smoother and quieter. Software-defined and autonomy-ready, the same fleet keeps improving over time.
why_navier_now.no_new_infrastructure: Navier rides on infrastructure that already exists — the harbours and jetties the public ferries already use. No new rights-of-way. Pioneer II needs only a berth pedestal; the Quanta-LR hybrid needs no charging infrastructure at all — decisive for remote islands.
why_navier_now.the_moment: Decarbonization mandates, a diesel fuel bill that constrains the network, and a platform now proven in Maldivian waters at national scale have converged. The public network is the natural next layer of a marine upgrade already underway.
